title: Track spending and find leaks
blurb: Small daily spends feel like nothing, until you add them up. Learn to track, spot patterns and lend wisely.
t1.title: The drip that fills the bucket
t1.hook: Meena buys a cold drink and chips for {daily} on the way home, every day. It feels like nothing.
t1.define: A **leak** is a small, regular spend you barely notice. One leak is small. Thirty days of it is not.
t1.analogy: A tap that drips a little all day still fills a bucket by night. Small spends fill the bucket the same way.
q1.prompt: Meena spends {daily} a day. How much is that over {monthDays} days? Type a number in rupees.
q1.hint: Multiply the daily amount by the number of days.
q2.prompt: Ravi says: it is only a few rupees, so it does not matter. What is wrong with that?
q2.hint: Think about how often the spend happens, not how big it is once.
q2.explain: The size of one spend is small. The number of times is what makes the total large.
q2.fb.a: It is true that one spend is tiny. But it repeats every day, so a small spend becomes a large sum.
q2.opt.b: Small spends repeat, so they add up to a large sum
q2.opt.c: Only big purchases ever need a budget
q2.opt.d: Spending is bad, so he must stop
t2.title: A whole year of it
t2.steps.1: Asha buys a snack for {daily2} every day.
t2.note: Not every small spend is a leak. A leak is a habit you do not really choose, like a daily snack bought by reflex.
q3.prompt: Back to Meena and her {daily} a day. How much does she spend on it in one year? Type a number in rupees.
q3.hint: Find the month first, then multiply by 12.
q3.explain: {perMonth} a month times 12 months is {perYear} a year.
q4.prompt: Which of these is most likely a leak?
q4.hint: A leak is small, regular, and hardly noticed.
q4.explain: Rent and fees are planned. The daily habit is small and easy to miss, so it leaks.
q4.opt.b: A tea and biscuits bought by habit every day
q4.opt.c: School fees, paid once a term
q4.opt.d: A festival gift, once a year
t3.title: Track for a week
t3.define: **Tracking** means writing down every rupee you spend for a week. A notebook or a phone note is enough. Do not judge, just write.
t3.steps.1: Write each spend the moment it happens.
t3.steps.2: At night, add up the day.
t3.steps.3: After seven days, look for the biggest and the most repeated spends.
t3.week: Ravi tracked his week. Mon {mon}, Tue {tue}, Wed {wed}, Thu {thu}, Fri {fri}, Sat {sat}, Sun {sun}. Most of it went on food and outings with friends.
q5.prompt: What did Ravi spend in the whole week? Add up all seven days.
q5.hint: Add the seven daily amounts one after another.
q6.prompt: What share of the week did Ravi spend on Saturday and Sunday together? Type a percentage.
q6.hint: Add Saturday and Sunday, then divide by the week total.
q6.explain: Saturday and Sunday add up to {weekend}. That is {weekendShare} of the week.
q7.prompt: What is the best next step for Ravi after seeing his week?
q7.hint: Tracking is for noticing, not for punishing yourself.
q7.explain: A pattern shows where to look. Keep what you value, and trim what you barely notice.
q7.opt.b: Look at the weekend spends and decide which ones he truly enjoys
q7.opt.c: Ignore the notes and carry on
q7.opt.d: Spend nothing on weekdays and more on weekends
t4.title: Lab: what does a leak cost?
t4.explore: Open the lab. Change the daily spend to see its cost over a month and a year. Then answer below.
q8.prompt: In the lab, set the daily spend to {labDaily}. What does it cost in a year? Type a number.
q8.hint: Read the red number in the lab.
q8.explain: {labDaily} a day is {labMonth} a month and {labYear} a year.
q9.prompt: In the lab, you halve the daily spend. What happens to the yearly cost?
q9.hint: Try it with the slider and compare the red numbers.
q9.explain: The year is just the day times a fixed number. Halve one and the other halves too.
t5.title: Lending to friends
t5.define: Lending small sums to friends is kind. Be plain about it: lend only what you can live without, and say when you need it back.
t5.note: Keep a short note: who, how much, the date, and when it will come back. A note protects the friendship, not only the money.
t5.mistake: Many people think a friend will surely return the money without being asked. Often they just forget. Asking politely is not rude.
q10.prompt: Ravi lent {lent} to friends in all. So far {back} has come back. How much is still owed to him?
q10.hint: Subtract what came back from what he lent.
q10.explain: {lent} minus {back} is {owed}. A note helps him remember it.
q11.prompt: Imran asks to borrow {ask}, but Meena needs that money for a bus pass next week. What is the best reply?
q11.hint: Be kind, be clear, and protect money you need.
q11.explain: A plain, small, dated loan keeps both the money and the friendship safe.
q11.opt.a: Lend it and hope he remembers
q11.fb.a: Hoping is not a plan. Without a date or a note, a kind loan often turns into a lost sum and an awkward silence.
q11.opt.b: Say what she can spare, agree a date, and write it down
q11.opt.c: Lend it and never mention it again
q12.prompt: Challenge: Meena cuts her daily {daily} habit to {cutTo}. How much does she save in a year, with {monthDays} days a month?
q12.hint: Find the daily saving first. Then multiply by the days in a month, then by 12.
q12.explain: She saves {saveDay} a day, {saveMonth} a month, and {saveYear} a year.
glossary.save_leak.def: A small, regular spend you barely notice that adds up.
glossary.save_tracking.def: Writing down what you spend so you can see where it goes.
glossary.save_pattern.def: A spend that repeats on certain days, places or moods.
